questions.q: Why must wei amounts be typed as bigint instead of number in TypeScript?
options: number is a 64-bit float that loses precision above 2^53, and wei amounts (e.g. 1 ETH = 10^18 wei) routinely exceed that
bigint runs faster than number in all cases
TypeScript doesn't allow number literals with underscores
wei amounts are always negative, which number can't represent
questions.explain: A JavaScript number can't precisely represent integers above 2^53, and wei values regularly exceed that threshold, so bigint (with a trailing n literal) is required.

questions.q: What does the template literal type `type Address = `0x${string}`;` actually enforce?
options: That the string is converted to a number automatically
Nothing at runtime — the value is still a string; the check only happens at compile time
That the value is a bigint
That the address is checksummed
questions.explain: Template literal types are a compile-time-only narrowing of string — they catch malformed literals and mismatched assignments while type-checking, but produce a plain string at runtime.

questions.q: In the lesson's Transaction interface, why is `to: Address | null` instead of just `to: Address`?
options: Because TypeScript requires every field to be nullable
Because Address can never be assigned directly
Because a contract-creation transaction has no destination address
Because null makes the interface compile faster
questions.explain: A contract-creation transaction genuinely has no `to` address, so modeling it as nullable forces code to handle that real case instead of assuming every transaction has a destination.

questions.q: What problem does a branded type solve that a plain template literal type alone does not?
options: It makes the string type faster at runtime
It converts the string into a bigint automatically
It removes the need for the 0x prefix
It prevents two different string-based types (like Address and TxHash) from being accidentally interchanged, even though both match the same `0x...` pattern
questions.explain: A template literal type only checks the string's shape, not what it represents — a branded type adds a fake compile-time tag so an Address and a TxHash can't be passed for each other, even though both are 0x-prefixed strings.

questions.q: Does the "__brand" tag used in a branded type exist at runtime, in the compiled JavaScript?
options: Yes — it's stored as an extra property on every string
No — it's erased during compilation and costs nothing at runtime
Yes — it's compiled into a separate bigint field
Only in strict mode
questions.explain: Branded types are a pure TypeScript compile-time construct; the brand is erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript, so there's no runtime cost or extra property.
